import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The Goormaghtigh conjecture

A repunit is a number whose digits in some base are all $1$. Here a nontrivial representation has
at least three digits. The Goormaghtigh conjecture says that $31$ and $8191$ are the only numbers
having nontrivial repunit representations in two different bases.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goormaghtigh_conjecture)
* J. Grantham,
  [No new Goormaghtigh primes up to $10^{700}$](https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/y98/y98.pdf)
-/

namespace Goormaghtigh

/-- The repunit with `digits` digits in the given base, expressed without division. -/
def repunit (base digits : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ∑ i ∈ Finset.range digits, base ^ i

/-- A number having repunit representations of at least three digits in two distinct bases. -/
def IsGoormaghtighNumber (N : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ base₁ base₂ digits₁ digits₂ : ℕ,
    2 ≤ base₁ ∧ 2 ≤ base₂ ∧ base₁ ≠ base₂ ∧
      3 ≤ digits₁ ∧ 3 ≤ digits₂ ∧
        repunit base₁ digits₁ = N ∧ repunit base₂ digits₂ = N

/-- The only Goormaghtigh numbers are $31$ and $8191$. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem goormaghtigh_conjecture (N : ℕ) (hN : IsGoormaghtighNumber N) :
    N = 31 ∨ N = 8191 := by
  sorry

/-- The number $31$ is a repunit in bases $2$ and $5$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isGoormaghtighNumber_31 : IsGoormaghtighNumber 31 := by
  refine ⟨2, 5, 5, 3, ?_⟩
  norm_num [repunit]

/-- The number $8191$ is a repunit in bases $2$ and $90$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isGoormaghtighNumber_8191 : IsGoormaghtighNumber 8191 := by
  refine ⟨2, 90, 13, 3, ?_⟩
  norm_num [repunit]

/-- Allowing two-digit repunits would make $13$ a representation in two distinct bases. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem repunit_two_digits : repunit 3 3 = 13 ∧ repunit 12 2 = 13 := by
  norm_num [repunit]

end Goormaghtigh

reformulations.difference: Uses finite geometric sums and unordered distinct natural-number bases rather than rational quotients with the convention x > y > 1 and n > m > 2.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For b ≥ 2, the finite sum is exactly (b^d−1)/(b−1), with a nonzero denominator. The natural-number bounds capture precisely the permitted positive integers. Reordering the two representations so that x > y loses nothing; monotonicity of the sum in its base and length forces m < n. Proved the predicate's equivalence to the ordered rational-quotient formulation in Review.predicate_iff_ordered_rat_equation in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: Classifies the common value N by a forward implication rather than enumerating the two ordered solution quadruples or stating a biconditional.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The proved examples supply the converse, so the implication is equivalent to IsGoormaghtighNumber N ↔ N = 31 ∨ N = 8191. Moreover, any admissible representation of N ≤ 8191 has base ≤ 90 and length ≤ 13. An exhaustive Lean `decide` proof on these bounds verifies that 31 has exactly the representations (base,length) = (2,5),(5,3), and 8191 has exactly (2,13),(90,3). Consequently the value classification is equivalent to the source's ordered quadruple classification. Both equivalences were proved in the scratch file without using the conjecture's `sorry`.

sources_consulted: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goormaghtigh_conjecture — full article, including the repunit formulation and partial results.
J. Grantham, No new Goormaghtigh primes up to 10^700, Integers 24 (2024), A98. https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/y98/y98.pdf
Y. Bugeaud and T. N. Shorey, On the Diophantine equation (x^m−1)/(x−1)=(y^n−1)/(y−1), Pacific Journal of Mathematics 207 (2002), 61–75, §§1–2. https://msp.org/pjm/2002/207-1/pjm-v207-n1-p04-s.pdf
review.notes: Checked all six declarations. Boundary evaluations confirm the geometric-sum conventions; the predicate excludes bases 0 and 1 and lengths below 3, implies N ≥ 7, and does not hold for 13. All three test theorems were independently checked and have no sorryAx dependency. The scratch file compiles successfully. Wikipedia still records the general conjecture as unsolved, consistent with `research open`. Source caveat: Grantham's displayed Conjecture 1 prints y > x together with n > m, an inconsistent ordering. Its abstract and introduction state the intended repunit conjecture correctly; Bugeaud–Shorey explicitly confirms that y > x forces m > n. This source typo is not a defect in the Lean file.
